Actually, for reverse polarity protection, a common approach is to use a P-channel MOSFET in the high side with the gate pulled to GND. When the input is correct, the body diode conducts, and then the gate is pulled low (relative to source), turning on the MOSFET. Actually, for reverse polarity protection, a common approach is to use a P-channel MOSFET in the high side with the gate pulled to GND. When the input is correct, the body diode conducts, and then the gate is pulled low (relative to source), turning on the MOSFET. When the input is reversed, the body diode blocks, and the gate is at the same potential as the source (via the resistor), so the MOSFET stays off.

For an N-channel MOSFET in the high side, you'd need a charge pump to pull the gate above the source. Hmm.

Actually, for reverse polarity protection, a common approach is to use a P-channel MOSFET in the high side with the gate pulled to GND. When the input is correct, the body diode conducts, and then the gate is pulled low (relative to source), turning on the MOSFET. Actually, for reverse polarity protection, a common approach is to use a P-channel MOSFET in the high side with the gate pulled to GND. When the input is correct, the body diode conducts, and then the gate is pulled low (relative to source), turning on the MOSFET. Actually, for reverse polarity protection, a common approach is to use a P-channel MOSFET in the high side with the gate pulled to GND. When the input is correct, the body diode conducts, and then the gate is pulled low (relative to source), turning on the MOSFET. When the input is reversed, the body diode blocks, and the gate is at the same potential as the source (via the resistor), so the MOSFET stays off.

For an N-channel MOSFET in the high side, you'd need a charge pump to pull the gate above the source. Hmm.

Actually, for reverse polarity protection, a common approach is to use a P-channel MOSFET in the high side with the gate pulled to GND. When the input is correct, the body diode conducts, and then the gate is pulled low (relative to source), turning on the MOSFET. Actually, for reverse polarity protection, a common approach is to use a P-channel MOSFET in the high side with the gate pulled to GND. When the input is correct, the body diode conducts, and then the gate is pulled low (relative to source), turning on the MOSFET. When the input is reversed, the body diode blocks, and the gate is at the same potential as the source (via the resistor), so the MOSFET stays off.

For an N-channel MOSFET in the high side, you'd need a charge pump to pull the gate above the source. Hmm.

Actually, for reverse polarity protection, a common approach is to use a P-channel MOSFET in the high side with the gate pulled to GND. When the input is correct, the body diode conducts, and then the gate is pulled low (relative to source), turning on the MOSFET. Actually, for reverse polarity protection, a common approach is to use a P-channel MOSFET in the high side with the gate pulled to GND. When the input is correct, the body diode conducts, and then the gate is pulled low (relative to source), turning on the MOSFET. Actually, for reverse polarity protection, a common approach is to use a P-channel MOSFET in the high side with the gate pulled to GND. When the input is correct, the body diode conducts, and then the gate is pulled low (relative to source), turning on the MOSFET. When the input is reversed, the body diode blocks, and the gate is at the same potential as the source (via the resistor), so the MOSFET stays off.

For an N-channel MOSFET in the high side, you'd need a charge pump to pull the gate above the source. Hmm.

Actually, for reverse polarity protection, a common approach is to use a P-channel MOSFET in the high side with the gate pulled to GND. When the input is correct, the body diode conducts, and then the gate is pulled low (relative to source), turning on the MOSFET. Actually, for reverse polarity protection, a common approach is to use a P-channel MOSFET in the high side with the gate pulled to GND. When the input is correct, the body diode conducts, and then the gate is pulled low (relative to source), turning on the MOSFET. When the input is reversed, the body diode blocks, and the gate is at the same potential as the source (via the resistor), so the MOSFET stays off.

Actually, for reverse polarity protection, a common approach is to use a P-channel MOSFET in the high side with the gate pulled to GND. When the input is correct, the body diode conducts, and then the gate is pulled low (relative to source), turning on the MOSFET. When the input is reversed, the body diode blocks, and the gate is at the same potential as the source (via the resistor), so the MOSFET stays off.

For an N-channel MOSFET in the high side, you'd need a charge pump to pull the gate above the source. Hmm.

Actually, for reverse polarity protection, a common approach is to use a P-channel MOSFET in the high side with the gate pulled to GND. When the input is correct, the body diode conducts, and then the gate is pulled low (relative to source), turning on the MOSFET. Actually, for reverse polarity protection, a common approach is to use a P-channel MOSFET in the high side with the gate pulled to GND. When the input is correct, the body diode conducts, and then the gate is pulled low (relative to source), turning on the MOSFET. When the input is reversed, the body diode blocks, and the gate is at the same potential as the source (via the resistor), so the MOSFET stays off.
